```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, dpi = 120)
```

**Data:** 120 Great Barrier Reef survey sites (2012). A teaching extract of the AIMS Long-Term Monitoring Program visual census fish dataset: *Plectropomus* (coral trout) counts summed over five transects per site, with sites grouped into Northern, Central and Southern latitude bands. Data sourced from the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS), [dataset link](https://apps.aims.gov.au/metadata/view/5be0b340-4ade-11dc-8f56-00008a07204e).

## 1. Executive summary

In 2012, divers are program to surveyed 120 reef sites along the Great Barrier Reef to count coral trout. The program manager would like to know how the counts are different among three latitude bands and between reefs open to fishing and no-take zones, and all this whether due of the zone difference and the latitude.

Generalised linear model is used to count the data where it'll assumed the variance of a count equal to its mean. Since there is data that violate the assumption, model refitting is then used to allow for extra variability which widens all reported uncertainty.

Southern sites hold about 4 times as many coral trout as Northern sites. No-take sites hold about 1.8 times as many coral trout as sites that are fishing allowed, somewhere between 1.25 and 2.5 times, and the same multiplier applies in all regions. The analysis only covers a single year, so it cannot predict whether things are going to get better or worse.

## 2. Problem and data

Objectives:

- estimate the count for each region and zone
- test whether an interaction is needed
- report the zone comparison with a 95% confidence interval

`coral_trout` = a non-negative integer count with no upper limit that is recorded once per site

`latitude_band` (Northern, Central, Southern) and `zone` (Open, No-take) = this is the explanatory variables with Northern and Open as references, so every number will be compared with a Northern open site.

One row is one site and one count is five equal-length transects added up. Each site has the same five and totals compare fairly. This is observational since reefs weren't randomly assigned their zoning.

```{r}
#| label: load-data-real
reef <- read.csv("aims_coral_trout_sites_2012.csv")

reef$latitude_band <- factor(
  reef$latitude_band,
  levels = c("Northern", "Central", "Southern")
)
reef$zone <- factor(
  reef$zone,
  levels = c("Open", "No-take")
)

dim(reef)
str(reef)
colSums(is.na(reef))
sum(duplicated(reef$site))
table(reef$latitude_band, reef$zone)
```

Hence it is a balanced design confirming there is 120 rows and 4 columns, no missing values and no repeated site with 18 sites per zone in the Northern and Central bands and 24 in the Southern.

## 3. Exploratory analysis

```{r}
#| label: tbl-groups
#| tbl-cap: "coral trout counts by latitude band and zone"

grp <- aggregate(coral_trout ~ latitude_band + zone, data = reef,
                 FUN = function(x) c(n = length(x), mean = mean(x),
                                     var = var(x), median = median(x),
                                     min = min(x), max = max(x)))
grp <- do.call(data.frame, grp)
names(grp) <- c("band", "zone", "n", "mean", "var", "median", "min", "max")
grp$var_mean_ratio <- grp$var / grp$mean
knitr::kable(grp[order(grp$band, grp$zone), ], digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-hist
#| fig-cap: "coral trout counts distribution across all 120 sites"
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4

hist(reef$coral_trout, breaks = seq(0, 65, by = 5), col = "grey80",
     main = "Site-level coral trout counts, 2012",
     xlab = "Coral trout per site (five transects)", ylab = "Number of sites")
rug(reef$coral_trout)
```

Figure 1 shows long tail stretching right with counts bunch up near zero, 13 sites recorded none, one site hit 61. That alone ruled out a normal linear model as the constant variance from Table 1 contradicts with group variances rise with group means from 3.8 to 202. But every variance-to-mean ratio exceeds 1, from 1.5 to 12.9, so the Poisson equality of mean and variance may be too strict.

```{r}
#| label: fig-strip
#| fig-cap: "Individual site counts within each latitude band and zone"
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5

glev <- c("N Open", "C Open", "S Open", "N No-take", "C No-take", "S No-take")
reef$grp <- factor(paste(substr(reef$latitude_band, 1, 1), reef$zone), levels = glev)
set.seed(1)
par(mar = c(5, 4.5, 3, 1))
stripchart(coral_trout ~ grp, data = reef, vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter",
           jitter = 0.15, pch = 1, col = "grey30", las = 1, xaxt = "n",
           xlab = "", ylab = "Coral trout per site (five transects)",
           main = "Site counts by latitude band and zone")
gm <- tapply(reef$coral_trout, reef$grp, mean)
points(seq_along(gm), gm, pch = 4, col = "red", cex = 1.6, lwd = 2)
gn <- table(reef$grp)
axis(1, at = seq_along(gn), labels = glev, las = 1, cex.axis = 0.85)
mtext(paste0("n=", as.vector(gn)), side = 1, at = seq_along(gn), line = 2, cex = 0.75)
mtext("N = Northern, C = Central, S = Southern", side = 1, line = 3.4, cex = 0.8)
legend("topleft", pch = 4, col = "red", pt.lwd = 2, legend = "group mean", bty = "n")
par(mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 4.1, 2.1))
```

Figure 2 shows red crosses mark as group means and sizes then vertical spread within group is wide, especially in the Southern band (Southern no-take group holds two high scores at 45 and 61).

```{r}
#| label: fig-interaction
#| fig-cap: "interaction plot of log group mean counts"
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5

interaction.plot(reef$latitude_band, reef$zone, log(reef$coral_trout + 0.5),
                 fun = mean, type = "b", pch = c(19, 17), col = c("darkorange", "steelblue"),
                 lwd = 2, las = 1, trace.label = "Zone",
                 xlab = "Latitude band", ylab = "Mean of log(count + 0.5)",
                 main = "Interaction plot on the log scale")
```

From Figure 3, it's shown parallel lines would shows a multiplicative zone effect across bands and the Southern gap is wider than the two. The model is additive which means parallel lines have no interaction, but it shows they are not parallel. Therefore, the no-take zone advantage is wider in the Southern band.

## 4. Initial GLM: Poisson

**Model:**

Let $Y_i$ be the count at site $i$, $i = 1, \dots, 120$, with $\mu_i = E(Y_i)$:

$$Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_i), \qquad Y_1, \dots, Y_{120} \text{ independent.}$$

Poisson only ever produces whole non-negative numbers with no upper bound with $\text{Var}(Y_i) = V(\mu_i) = \mu_i$, which is exactly what a fish count is. Fish behave like events in a fixed sampling window along the fixed-length transects. Poisson ties spread to average which variance equals the mean.

**Assumption:**

Sites don't influence each other, they're independent and once site's region and zone are known, nothing else systematically changes its count. The equality $\text{Var}(Y_i) = \mu_i$ follows from these.

**Link:**

The canonical log link $g(\mu) = \log \mu$ is used. Since $\eta_i$ ranges over the real line while $\mu_i = e^{\eta_i} > 0$ always, no coefficients can give a negative or zero fitted mean, which an identity link cannot guarantee. The log link is also multiplicative, so each exponentiated coefficient is a rate ratio.

**Linear predictor:**

With Northern and Open as references, let $C_i = 1$ if Central, $S_i = 1$ if Southern, and $N_i = 1$ if no-take:

$$\log \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 C_i + \beta_2 S_i + \beta_3 N_i + \beta_4 C_i N_i + \beta_5 S_i N_i.$$

```{r}
#| label: fit-m1
m1 <- glm(coral_trout ~ latitude_band * zone, family = poisson(link = "log"),
          data = reef)
summary(m1)

# rate ratios: exponentiated coefficients
knitr::kable(data.frame(term = names(coef(m1)),
                        estimate = round(coef(m1), 4),
                        rate_ratio = round(exp(coef(m1)), 3)),
             row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Interaction-model coefficients and their rate ratios.")
```

**Coefficients.** $\hat\beta_0 = 0.916$ is the log expected count at a Northern open site, which therefore holds $e^{0.916} = 2.5$ fish. The rest are log rate ratios: $\hat\beta_1 = 0.085$ gives $1.09$ and $\hat\beta_2 = 1.126$ gives $3.08$, so Central and Southern open sites hold 9% and about three times more. $\hat\beta_3 = 0.304$ gives $1.36$, the no-take-to-open ratio in the Northern band alone; the interactions change it to $e^{\beta_3 + \beta_4} = 1.12$ in the Central band and $e^{\beta_3 + \beta_5} = 2.03$ in the Southern. No single coefficient therefore answers the client's zone question.

## 5. Comparing initial models

$$\log \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 C_i + \beta_2 S_i + \beta_3 N_i.$$

Since it is nested, so $H_0: \beta_4 = \beta_5 = 0$ is tested at the 5% level by difference in deviance and it's referred to a chi-squared distribution.

```{r}
#| label: fit-m0
m0 <- glm(coral_trout ~ latitude_band + zone, family = poisson(link = "log"),
          data = reef)
anova(m0, m1, test = "Chisq")
AIC(m0, m1)
```

The result shows the deviance drops by 9.4 on 2 degrees of freedom with $p = 0.009$. AIC also valid since Poisson has a genuine likelihood and also prefers the interaction model (939.3 vs 944.7).

Both criteria rest on $\text{Var}(Y_i) = \mu_i$. If the true variance exceeds the mean, the deviance difference is inflated and the p-value too small, flagging an interaction the data do not support, a risk the ratios in Table 1 already suggest.

## 6. Checking dispersion

The dispersion is estimated from the Pearson residuals of the interaction model. With $r_i^P = (y_i - \hat\mu_i)/\sqrt{\hat\mu_i}$,

$$\hat\phi = \frac{X^2}{n - p} = \frac{1}{n-p}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{(y_i - \hat\mu_i)^2}{\hat\mu_i},$$

with $n - p = 120 - 6 = 114$ residual degrees of freedom.

```{r}
#| label: dispersion
pear <- residuals(m1, type = "pearson")
X2 <- sum(pear^2)
dfres <- df.residual(m1)
round(c(X2 = X2, df = dfres, phi_hat = X2 / dfres), 3)

# Goodness of fit: both statistics against chi-squared on 114 df
gof <- data.frame(
  statistic = c("Residual deviance", "Pearson X^2"),
  value     = round(c(deviance(m1), X2), 2),
  df        = dfres,
  p_value   = signif(c(pchisq(deviance(m1), dfres, lower.tail = FALSE),
                       pchisq(X2, dfres, lower.tail = FALSE)), 3)
)
knitr::kable(gof, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Goodness-of-fit statistics for the Poisson interaction model.")
```

The Pearson dispersion estimate is $\hat\phi = X^2/(n-p) = 613.0/114 = 5.38$. If Poisson were right this should sit near 1, but it's over five times that. Goodness of fit agrees where the residual deviance is 570.6 on 114 degrees of freedom, $p < 10^{-5}$ against $\chi^2_{114}$ and the Pearson statistic gives the same verdict which both should land near 114 if the model fits. These chi-squared approximations get rough when fitted means are small and results sit near 2, but a ratio of 5.4 is far too large to blame on that.

With two factors and their interaction, the model already reproduces all six group averages exactly, so no rearrangement of the predictors can reduce the leftover variation. Poisson standard errors are too small (2.32). Every z-statistic is inflated by that same factor, so Section 5 test rejected far too easily and its decision can't stand.

## 7. Handling overdispersion and final model

```{r}
#| label: fit-quasi
q1 <- glm(coral_trout ~ latitude_band * zone, family = quasipoisson(link = "log"),
          data = reef)
q0 <- glm(coral_trout ~ latitude_band + zone, family = quasipoisson(link = "log"),
          data = reef)
summary(q1)
anova(q0, q1, test = "F")
```

**Valid tools:**

Quasi-likelihood has no full likelihood, so AIC is undefined and R prints `AIC: NA`, and the likelihood ratio and chi-squared deviance tests are unavailable for the same reason. The F test is the valid comparison for nested quasi-likelihood models.

Testing $H_0: \beta_4 = \beta_5 = 0$ gives $F = 0.874$ on 2 and 114 degrees of freedom, $p = 0.42$. Therefore interaction in Section 5 was the result of the Poisson variance assumption.

```{r}
#| label: fit-nb
#| message: false
library(MASS)
nb1 <- glm.nb(coral_trout ~ latitude_band * zone, data = reef)
nb0 <- glm.nb(coral_trout ~ latitude_band + zone, data = reef)
anova(nb0, nb1)
round(c(AIC_nb_additive = AIC(nb0), AIC_nb_interaction = AIC(nb1),
        theta = nb0$theta), 2)
```

By assuming $\text{Var}(Y_i) = \mu_i + \mu_i^2/\theta$, negative binomial cross-check has a genuine likelihood, so the likelihood ratio test and AIC both agree that interaction gives $p = 0.31$ and AIC prefers additive model (654.8 vs 656.5).

Hence the final model is selected by using quasi-Poisson additive model,
$$\log \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 C_i + \beta_2 S_i + \beta_3 N_i, \qquad \text{Var}(Y_i) = \phi\mu_i,$$
with $\hat\phi = 5.40$, preferred to the negative binomial because it assumes only a mean and a variance function.

```{r}
#| label: final-model
qf <- glm(coral_trout ~ latitude_band + zone, family = quasipoisson(link = "log"),
          data = reef)
summary(qf)
```

## 8. Diagnostics and alternatives

```{r}
#| label: fig-diag
#| fig-cap: "Diagnostic for the final quasi-Poisson additive model."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

rstd <- rstandard(qf, type = "deviance")
hlev <- hatvalues(qf)
cook <- cooks.distance(qf)
flag <- abs(rstd) > 2

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 3, 1))

etahat <- predict(qf, type = "link")
plot(etahat, rstd, pch = 1, col = "grey30", las = 1,
     xlim = range(etahat) + c(-0.15, 0.45),
     xlab = "Fitted linear predictor", ylab = "Standardised deviance residual",
     main = "(a) Residuals vs linear predictor")
abline(h = c(-2, 0, 2), lty = c(2, 1, 2), col = c("red", "black", "red"))
lines(lowess(etahat, rstd), col = "blue", lwd = 2)
text(etahat[flag], rstd[flag], reef$site[flag], pos = 4, cex = 0.7)

qqnorm(rstd, main = "(b) QQ plot of standardised deviance residuals", las = 1,
       pch = 1, col = "grey30")
qqline(rstd, col = "red")

plot(hlev, type = "h", las = 1, xlab = "Site index", ylab = "Leverage",
     main = "(c) Leverage", ylim = c(0, max(hlev, 2 * mean(hlev)) * 1.15))
abline(h = 2 * mean(hlev), col = "red", lty = 2)

plot(cook, type = "h", las = 1, xlab = "Site index", ylab = "Cook's distance",
     main = "(d) Cook's distance")
abline(h = 4 / nrow(reef), col = "red", lty = 2)
text(which(cook > 0.1), cook[cook > 0.1], reef$site[cook > 0.1], pos = 4, cex = 0.7)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-flagged
#| tbl-cap: "Five sites with the largest standardised deviance residuals, shown with their fitted mean, leverage and Cook's distance"

diagtab <- data.frame(site = reef$site, band = reef$latitude_band, zone = reef$zone,
                      count = reef$coral_trout, fitted = round(fitted(qf), 2),
                      rstd = round(rstd, 2), leverage = round(hlev, 3),
                      cooks = round(cook, 3))
knitr::kable(diagtab[order(-abs(diagtab$rstd)), ][1:5, ], row.names = FALSE)
round(c(max_leverage = max(hlev),
        cutoff_2p_n = 2 * length(coef(qf)) / nrow(reef),
        max_cooks = max(cook), cutoff_4_n = 4 / nrow(reef)), 4)
```

Based on panel (a) from Figure 4 shows no curvature and no funnel which means log link and additive structure fit nicely. With 3 sites exceed $|r| = 2$ which all is from Southern no-take zone (AIMS022 at 3.92, AIMS024 at 2.75 and AIMS005 at $-2.39$), all listed in Table 2. With 120 sites, it is expected roughly 5 to land outside $\pm 2$ by chance alone, so three is fewer than expected. The max leverage is 0.038 which is against the cutoff of $2p/n = 0.067$, so nothing is flagged and no site sits anywhere unusual. Two of largest Cook's distance flags (AIMS022 at 0.268 and AIMS024 at 0.114) also exceed the $4/n = 0.033$ screen, but sit far below 1.

```{r}
#| label: refit-drop
reef_no22 <- reef[reef$site != "AIMS022", ]
qf2 <- glm(coral_trout ~ latitude_band + zone, family = quasipoisson(link = "log"),
           data = reef_no22)
q2i <- glm(coral_trout ~ latitude_band * zone, family = quasipoisson(link = "log"),
           data = reef_no22)
round(summary(qf2)$coefficients, 4)
round(c(phi_full = summary(qf)$dispersion,
        phi_dropped = summary(qf2)$dispersion,
        RR_zone_full = exp(coef(qf)[["zoneNo-take"]]),
        RR_zone_dropped = exp(coef(qf2)[["zoneNo-take"]])), 3)
anova(qf2, q2i, test = "F")
```

Refitting without AIMS022 moves the no-take rate ratio from 1.76 to 1.59, still significant ($p = 0.005$), the interaction still non-significant ($F = 0.58$, $p = 0.56$) and dispersion falling from 5.40 to 4.38, so the site contributes to the overdispersion without creating it. No substantive conclusion changes, so it is retained; dropping high counts would bias the means downward.

**Alternatives:**

If use negative binomial, it'll give the same answers, and its $\theta$ of 1.58 predicts about 16 expected zeros against 13 (observed), so there is no zero-inflation problem. Better recommendation is need more information such as reef identity, habitat, reef-level etc, which would explain more detail instead of just absorbing it into $\phi$.

## 9. Estimates and uncertainty

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fitted
#| tbl-cap: "Fitted expected coral trout count per site (five transects) with 95% confidence intervals, from the final quasi-Poisson additive model."

newd <- expand.grid(latitude_band = levels(reef$latitude_band),
                    zone = levels(reef$zone))
pr <- predict(qf, newdata = newd, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE)
tcrit <- qt(0.975, df = df.residual(qf))

fittab <- data.frame(
  band = newd$latitude_band, zone = newd$zone,
  eta = round(pr$fit, 3), se_eta = round(pr$se.fit, 3),
  fitted_count = round(exp(pr$fit), 2),
  lower = round(exp(pr$fit - tcrit * pr$se.fit), 2),
  upper = round(exp(pr$fit + tcrit * pr$se.fit), 2)
)
knitr::kable(fittab[order(fittab$band, fittab$zone), ], row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: zone-ci
cf <- summary(qf)$coefficients
b_zone <- cf["zoneNo-take", "Estimate"]
se_zone <- cf["zoneNo-take", "Std. Error"]

# 95% CI on the linear predictor (log) scale
ci_link <- b_zone + c(-1, 1) * tcrit * se_zone
round(c(estimate_log = b_zone, se = se_zone,
        lower_log = ci_link[1], upper_log = ci_link[2]), 4)

# back-transformed to a rate ratio on the response scale
round(c(rate_ratio = exp(b_zone), lower = exp(ci_link[1]),
        upper = exp(ci_link[2])), 3)

# latitude band contrasts, both relative to Northern
for (nm in c("latitude_bandCentral", "latitude_bandSouthern")) {
  est <- cf[nm, "Estimate"]; se <- cf[nm, "Std. Error"]
  print(round(c(RR = exp(est), lower = exp(est - tcrit * se),
                upper = exp(est + tcrit * se)), 3))
}
```

Table 3 gives the fitted site means: about 2.1 fish at Northern and Central open sites, 8.5 at Southern open and 14.9 at Southern no-take, with wide intervals throughout.

**Zoning comparison:**

$\hat\beta_3 = 0.5652$ on the linear predictor scale, standard error 0.1743, on 116 residual degrees of freedom.

$$\hat\beta_3 \pm t_{0.975,116} \times \text{SE} = 0.5652 \pm 1.9806 \times 0.1743 = (0.220,\ 0.910).$$

Exponentiating both endpoints, valid because the exponential is monotonic:

$$e^{0.5652} = 1.76, \qquad \text{95\% CI } (1.25,\ 2.49).$$

In words, these no-take sites hold about 1.76 times as many coral trout as open sites (1.25 to 2.49). The naive Poisson fit would have reported 1.52 to 2.04 which the interval is 2.3 times too narrow.

In conclusion, latitude is mainly the reason where Southern sites hold 3.96 times as many as Northern (95% CI 2.43 to 6.45), while Central sits at 0.98 times Northern with an interval of 0.52 to 1.85, that comfortably contains 1. The no-take zone is also 1.76 times more applied in all three bands, no evidence after accounting for overdispersion that it varied with latitude ($F = 0.87$, $p = 0.42$).

Three conclusions to avoid. Zoning was not assigned, so 1.76 is not a measured effect of protection: no-take reefs may differ in habitat, remoteness or pre-existing abundance. The analysis covers 2012 alone and says nothing about trend. And no evidence of an interaction is not evidence of none, since with this much variability only a large difference between bands was detectable.

**Software.** R (R Core Team) with the base `stats` package and `MASS` (Venables and Ripley) for the negative binomial cross-check in Section 7.
